Reger: On the Theory of Modulation

All 100 examples from Beiträge zur Modulationslehre (1903), with Roman numerals under the notes

Every example from Max Reger’s modulation handbook (Beiträge zur Modulationslehre, 1903; in English as On the Theory of Modulation), from C major, C♯ major, A minor, C♭ major, D♭ minor and A♯ minor to every other key, each a few chords long, with the Roman-numeral analysis under the notes (When in Rome). Play each one.

In 1903 Max Reger published a short book of modulations: one hundred examples, each a few chords long, that get from one key to another, often a distant one, as quickly as possible. Most go by a pivot chord: a chord that belongs to both keys, very often the Neapolitan (N⁶) or a dominant of the dominant (V/V). Each new key is then confirmed with a cadence: Cad⁶₄ (I⁶₄), V, I.

The examples are grouped by the key they start from, in the book’s order. Where an example has an A and a B version, B goes to the minor key with the same tonic. How to read the labels and use the scores: Analysed Scores.

Things to find

  • The pivot: in each example, find the first chord after the new key is named. Which chord is it in the old key?
  • The Neapolitan: N⁶ appears in 45 of the examples, mostly the far ones (from C major to the sharp keys, 6–12 and 24–31, and all of 86–99 except 98). V/V appears in 25. In each, is it the pivot, or does it come after the new key is reached?
  • Enharmonic spellings: the far keys are written as they are named, so C♭ major and A♯ minor appear with all their flats and sharps. The keys B𝄫 major (21) and E♯ minor (30) are spelled out too.

NoteFor teachers
  • Source: the notes and analyses are the DDMAL Key Modulation Dataset’s encodings of Reger’s examples (Néstor Nápoles López and others), translated automatically to RomanText and copied into When in Rome. scripts/when-in-rome/build.mjs reads the MusicXML (src/reger), and every note was checked against music21’s reading of the same files.
  • Example 41 (C major to C♭ minor) has no notes in the corpus, only its analysis, which is printed in its place.
  • 46A and 46B number their first bar 0 in the analysis; the build counts it as bar 1, where its notes are.
  • Two corrections: in 38 the analysis names D♭ minor for the last three chords, where the notes (and the book’s title) are A♭ minor; in 45B it writes the last key as major, then labels its chord i. Both are corrected on the page, with a note under the example, by REGER_FIX in build.mjs; the corpus files are unchanged.
  • Otherwise not edited: the analyses are an automated translation and are shown as they are. In 56 and 70 they label every chord in the new key, without naming the starting key.
  • Headings take both keys from the book’s titles, not from the analysis.

For students

Gotham, Mark, et al. When in Rome: A Meta-Corpus of Functional Harmony. GitHub. github.com/MarkGotham/When-in-Rome. The analyses on this page (RomanText files), licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

Hutchinson, Robert. “Modulation.” Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom, ch. 22, U of Puget Sound. musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Modulation.html. Tonicization against modulation, closely related keys, diatonic and chromatic pivot chords, and direct, common-tone and sequential modulation.

Reger, Max. Beiträge zur Modulationslehre. C. F. Kahnt Nachfolger, 1903. Translated by John Bernhoff as On the Theory of Modulation, Kahnt, [1904?]; reprinted as Supplement to the Theory of Modulation, Dover, 2007. The book whose 100 examples are shown on the Reger page. Public domain (Reger died in 1916).

For teachers

Nápoles López, Néstor, et al. Key Modulation Dataset. GitHub (DDMAL). github.com/DDMAL/key_modulation_dataset. The encodings and analyses of the textbook examples, translated to RomanText by Nápoles López and copied into When in Rome.

Reger-Werkausgabe. “1903.” Max Reger: Biography. Max-Reger-Institut. www.maxreger.info/biography/1903. When Reger wrote the book and how it came to be published by Kahnt.
